source.title: Sparse Attention Decomposition Applied to Circuit Tracing

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports sparse decompositions of GPT-2 attention scores and discusses geometric ideas related to superposition, but it does not test feature superposition, capacity competition, SAE recovery, or the dimensionality of superposed features as defined by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures how many SVD orthogonal slices contribute to attention scores, and describes slice reuse for selected heads. These are results about sparse attention-score decomposition, not tests of the claim versions about features competing for representational capacity or being superposed. Intervention results concern circuit tracing and IOI performance, so they are not included as claim-version rows.
record.test_reason: The paper measures how sparsely GPT-2 small attention scores decompose into SVD slices of QK matrices, and uses this for circuit tracing. It runs no toy models and no SAEs, and measures no neuron polysemanticity or feature dimensionality. Section 6.1 only speculates, citing Toy Models' 'local, almost-orthogonal bases'. The authors also state they make a 'local non-superposition assumption'. No result bears on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that attention scores in GPT-2 small are typically sparsely constructed in the SVD basis of the QK matrices. They add that the resulting low-dimensional signals allow single-pass tracing of IOI head-to-head communication. Edge ablation and boosting validate these signals as causally affecting attention scores and IOI performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study decomposes attention-head QK computation with SVD and uses sparse slice contributions for circuit tracing; it does not implement the toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The number and identity of selected slices depend on the input and whether the head is firing; different slices are used in firing and non-firing cases. The study compares IOI prompts with non-specific text inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-2 small attention scores are sparsely built from a few QK SVD slices, typically 20 or fewer of 64. This holds on IOI and Pile inputs. Slice sets differ between heads and between firing and non-firing cases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In GPT-2, attention scores are sparsely decomposable in the SVD basis of each head's QK matrix, with input- and condition-dependent slice sets.

fits_no_version.finding: Projecting residuals onto the 12 consensus V-subspace slices of head (9,9) separates name tokens from non-names (Figure 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: QK singular-vector subspaces of attention heads carry interpretable, task-relevant token features.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to GPT-2 small and selected IOI and non-specific input sets. The slice-selection/noise-separation rule is heuristic, and per-head distributions are shown in plots without tabulated values or reported uncertainty. The study does not test feature superposition or feature capacity claims.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version rows were applicable. Omitted circuit-tracing intervention outcomes and the name-token projection result because they concern IOI circuit causality or a semantic signal, not the claim versions; intervention plots are in §5.4 and the Appendix, and the name-token result is in §5.2 and Figure 9.

untested.parts: No toy networks, feature-versus-dimension sweep, sparsity transition or geometry.
No neuron polysemanticity or capacity competition measured.
No alternative causes of polysemanticity examined.
No measure of feature spread across neurons, and no SAE recovery. The SVD-slice sparsity concerns attention-score construction, not features in the residual.
No SAE features evaluated. SAEs are mentioned only as complementary future work.
The paper notes head (4,11) appears to use a single slice, but it does not test whether superposed features are 1-D or multi-dimensional.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (discusses) and tranche (T6) are confirmed. Superposition appears only as speculative motivation in §6.1. The phrase 'superposition effect' in the appendix refers to non-additive ablation effects, not feature superposition. Intervention results were correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-count-versus-dimension comparison, feature overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transition is tested.
No neuron polysemanticity, capacity competition, or importance-based allocation of dedicated versus shared dimensions is tested.
No alternative cause of polysemantic neurons, or evidence about whether polysemanticity indicates superposition, is tested.
The study examines GPT-2 attention-score decompositions, not feature spread across neurons or features recovered with an SAE.
No SAE features or claims about their completeness, stability, or canonical status are evaluated.
Rank-1 SVD slices are measured as components of attention-score computation, but the study does not test whether superposed model features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compared the SVD slices used in attention scores across prompts for a firing head.
rows.measure: Consistency and number of slices used across prompts
rows.value: About 6 slices are consistently used; typically |Sij| is 20 or less, often 2 or 3
rows.note: The authors identify this as an S-inhibition head.
rows.check: The value mixes two sources. 'About 6 slices' is specific to head (8,6) (§5.1). 'Typically 20 or less, often 2 or 3' is a general statement across heads (§4.1), not a result for (8,6).

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compared the SVD slices used in attention scores across prompts for a firing head.
rows.measure: Consistency and number of slices used across prompts
rows.value: Primarily a single slice is used
rows.note: The authors describe this as consistent with the head detecting adjacent tokens.
